passage:
Pantry, after the Monday review.

Pradeep: You okay?
Siddharth: Fine. (pause) My face is still burning. He read my report aloud in that voice and said, "Is this what they teach at your college?" Everyone laughed. He calls it directness.
Pradeep: I saw. That wasn't directness, that was mocking. The mistakes in the report you can fix. The way he said it is on him.
Siddharth: I froze. I couldn't say a word.
Pradeep: Most people do. Write it down today: the date, what he said, who was in the room. Every time.
Siddharth: For what?
Pradeep: For when you talk to HR, or to me again. And keep your CV fresh, quietly.
Siddharth: So it's not just me being oversensitive?
Pradeep: No. Find me on Wednesday and we'll go through it together.

qa.q: What does the boss call his mocking?
What was Siddharth worried about when asking whether it was just oversensitivity?
qa.a: Siddharth worried that the hurt might be an overreaction, which shows how much the mockery had shaken Siddharth's confidence.
Pradeep suggested writing down the date, the words and who was there each time, keeping the CV fresh quietly, and talking to HR or to Pradeep.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the boss's behaviour?
qa.a: Pradeep sees it as mocking rather than directness, and says the way he said it is on the boss, not on Siddharth's report.

grounding: A boss mocks Siddharth in front of the team and calls it directness; a trusted senior helps see it as the boss's conduct and suggests notes, HR and exits.

passage: Note for my own file, Thursday. Manjula, senior analyst. At this morning's team meeting, Mr. Rao held up Siddharth's report and said, 'My nephew in Class 8 could do better. I'm just being direct.' Some people laughed. Siddharth, who joined as a trainee in June, went red to the ears and stared at the table without moving. It is the third time this month I have seen Mr. Rao do this to him. After the meeting I found him at the pantry and told him plainly that this was Mr. Rao's behaviour, not a measure of his work. I suggested he write down each incident with the date and the words, and offered to go with him to HR next week as a witness. Before leaving he asked if I knew of openings in other teams or firms; I said I'd keep an ear out. I have started noting the dates myself.

qa.a: Siddharth joined as a trainee in June.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling as he stared at the table?
qa.a: Siddharth felt humiliated and frozen, red to the ears after being mocked in front of the team.
Writing down each incident with dates, going to HR with a witness, and keeping an ear out for openings protect Siddharth and build options.

qa.q: How does Mr. Rao seem to see his own comments?
qa.a: Mr. Rao presents the mockery as just being direct, ignoring how it humiliates a new trainee.

grounding: A senior colleague's note records a boss mocking a trainee in public, and the steps of naming it as the boss's conduct, keeping dated notes, going to HR and looking for exits.

passage: Friday. Diary, Anirban here, and my face still feels hot. Today Mr. Kapoor made me read my client email aloud in the meeting and then said, 'Now say it in English,' and everyone laughed. He calls it 'toughening us up'. I just stood there. In the washroom I nearly typed my resignation on my phone. Instead I called Anjali, my college friend who's been working two years longer than me. She said three things: write down what happened today with the time and exact words; talk to Ruchika-ma'am from the other team, who everyone trusts; and meanwhile update my CV without telling anyone. So I've written it all below: 11:20 a.m., conference room B, his words, who was there. It's his behaviour, Anjali said, not my worth. I'm trying to believe that. Monday: Ruchika-ma'am. Tonight: CV.

qa.q: Where and when did the meeting take place?
qa.a: At 11:20 a.m., in conference room B.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling in the washroom?
qa.a: Anirban felt humiliated and upset enough to nearly type a resignation.

qa.q: Which of Anjali's suggestions protects Anirban most, and why?
qa.a: Writing down the time and exact words, because it creates a record Ruchika-ma'am or HR can act on, while the CV quietly builds an exit.

qa.q: How does Mr. Kapoor describe his own behaviour?
qa.a: Mr. Kapoor calls it 'toughening us up', framing public mockery as training.

grounding: A diary records a boss humiliating Anirban in a meeting, and a friend's advice to note the details, talk to a trusted senior and quietly prepare an exit.
